title: Indian Student Applications to US Undergraduate Programs Drop 15% Amid Visa Crackdown
excerpt: A Common App report shows Indian applicants fell sharply in 2025-26 as tighter immigration rules, a proposed $100,000 OPT fee, and four-year visa caps push families toward alternative destinations.
body:
• Indian undergraduate applications to US colleges fell 15% in 2025-26 compared with the previous year, according to a Common App report covering more than 1,100 institutions.
  • Overall international applications dropped 10% through March 1 for the 2026-27 academic year — the steepest decline on record.
  • New visa rules capping student stays at four years and a proposed $100,000 OPT fee are fueling uncertainty among prospective students and their families.
  • The UK, Germany, and France are emerging as alternative destinations as Indian students recalculate the return on a US degree.

The number of Indian students applying for undergraduate admission at American universities fell 15% in the 2025-26 application cycle compared with the previous year, according to a report by Common App, the nonprofit platform used by more than 1,100 US institutions.

The decline is part of a broader pullback in international interest in American higher education. Through March 1, international applications for the 2026-27 academic year dropped 10% — the steepest decline Common App has ever recorded. India, the largest source of international students in the United States with more than 363,000 enrolled during the 2024-25 academic year, saw one of the sharpest country-level drops.

What's Driving the Decline

Several policy shifts have made the US a less predictable destination for Indian students and their families.

https://x.com/firstpost/status/2092065849096192257

In July 2026, the Department of Homeland Security finalized rules replacing the longstanding "duration of status" framework — which allowed international students to remain in the country for the length of their academic program — with fixed admission periods capped at four years. Starting September 15, students needing additional time for program changes, academic delays, or authorized practical training will have to apply for extensions, adding administrative burden and cost.

The proposed $100,000 fee for international graduates seeking to use Optional Practical Training (OPT), the post-graduation work program that has long been a key draw for STEM students, has further rattled prospective applicants. While the fee remains under consideration, the possibility alone has shifted how families evaluate the return on a US degree.

"Over 40 per cent have seen their interest in studying in the US decrease in the past year, driven directly by visa policy and rising costs."

— Avnish Singhal, Head of Consumer Business, Emeritus

A separate report by NAFSA: Association of International Educators and research firm JB International projects up to 111,000 fewer international students at US universities in Fall 2026. International student registration dropped from an estimated 1.17 million in Fall 2025-26 to 1.06 million this year. The economic impact is tangible: international students contributed $41.77 billion to the US economy in 2025-26, a figure projected to fall to $38.37 billion in 2026-27.

The Broader Enrollment Picture

The undergraduate application decline sits alongside an overall erosion in Indian enrollment across US institutions. Data from the Student and Exchange Visitor Information System (SEVIS) shows the total number of Indian students in the US fell from 378,787 in February 2025 to 352,644 in February 2026 — a 6.9% decline spanning programs from primary school through doctoral studies.

A sustained pullback could hit institutions that have relied heavily on international enrollment, particularly in graduate STEM programs where Indian students are disproportionately represented. For universities already navigating funding pressures and declining domestic enrollment in some regions, losing a significant share of international applicants adds a financial strain that extends beyond admissions offices.

Families Look Beyond the US

The shift is not simply about students staying home. Education industry experts say the UK, Germany, and France are emerging as beneficiaries, offering clearer visa pathways, more predictable post-study work rights, and — in Germany's case — substantially lower tuition.

An upcoming Emeritus study surveying more than 1,000 Indians aged 15 to 28 found that over 40% reported decreased interest in studying in the US over the past year. Students are applying strategically across multiple countries rather than committing to a single destination, industry analysts say.

For Indian parents weighing a US undergraduate education — often a four-year commitment exceeding $200,000 — the calculus has changed. The four-year visa cap removes the flexibility that "duration of status" once provided. The OPT fee proposal threatens post-graduation plans. And the broader policy climate has introduced uncertainties that did not exist even two years ago.

The 15% drop in applications is an early signal. If the current policy direction holds, US universities could face deeper declines in coming admission cycles — and Indian families will continue redirecting their investment toward destinations that offer more stability for the price.
